This conversation centered on building out the complete web infrastructure for the Thessalonian Mandate Institute (TMI), a faith-based organization founded by Rickey Jay Bennett II in Austin, Texas, operating under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A). The person owns the domain thessalonian-mandate-institute.org through GoDaddy and worked through a full deployment pipeline: creating a GitHub account, making a repository named TMI-page, uploading an index.html file, enabling GitHub Pages, and attempting to connect the custom domain. GoDaddy's DNS wizard blocked direct DNS editing, so a Permanent (301) redirect was set as a temporary solution while DNS propagates.

The session covered a complete redesign of the TMI website with a specific visual aesthetic: gold, white, and soft blue tones with transparent faded edges, no hard lines, frosted glass cards, and fixed background images that stay stationary while content scrolls over them. Two background images were established — a sky with light rays for the ministry/donor/about sections, and a shepherd-leading-workers image for the school and curriculum sections. Image processing was done iteratively with saturation and opacity adjustments across multiple rounds until the person approved the look. A full Supabase backend was set up at project URL mwrazxkxmznvoijitqys.supabase.co for student accounts, applications, progress tracking, and messaging. The person reviewed a complete site build covering home, school with 16 free certification pathways, about, donor, contact, and student dashboard sections — but noted that Claude's Python f-string approach to generating HTML caused JavaScript syntax errors due to curly brace escaping conflicts. The person indicated they would learn to build it themselves going forward, and ended the session reviewing and partially debugging their own version of the application form code.

Key organizational details established: the founder holds all four current board positions (Minister, CEO, Secretary, Treasurer). Seventeen email addresses were documented for creation across leadership, functional, and future-hire roles. The full certification catalog was built from IBM SkillsBuild, Google Career Certificates via Coursera financial aid, Microsoft Learn Applied Skills, Fortinet NSE 1-3, and freeCodeCamp — all confirmed free with no calls or applications required to launch students immediately. The person communicates directly and prefers step-by-step instructions that assume no prior knowledge, and explicitly flagged when Claude over-explained or skipped steps.

Here is the full breakdown pulled directly from GoDaddy's own documentation. There are two different situations depending on what you already have, so read which one applies.

---

## Situation A — You Already Have a GoDaddy Hosting Plan (cPanel)

This is the standard path. If you bought a hosting plan along with the domain, here is the process:

1. Log into your GoDaddy account and go to your product page.
2. Under Web Hosting, next to the Web Hosting (cPanel) account you want to use, select **Manage**. Under Websites, select **File Manager** for your domain.
3. Navigate to the directory where you want to upload. By default, you will start in your primary root directory or addon domain root directory. Select **Upload**. Drag your files into **Drop files here to start uploading**. Or select **Select file**, choose the file you want to upload, and then select **Open**. When all your files reach 100%, your upload is complete.

The HTML file I built needs to be named **`index.html`** — that is the file the server will serve automatically when someone visits the domain root. Drop it directly into the `public_html` folder (that is your root directory).

---

## Situation B — You Only Own the Domain, No Hosting Plan

If you registered `thessalonian-mandate-institute.org` through GoDaddy but did not purchase a hosting plan, a domain alone cannot serve files. You have two options:

**Option 1 — Buy a GoDaddy hosting plan** (paid, ~$3–8/month)
GoDaddy offers Web Hosting (cPanel), which runs Linux on the server with cPanel access through the account Dashboard. Once purchased, it connects to your domain and you follow Situation A above.

**Option 2 — Free hosting, point your domain at it** (free)
Host the HTML file on GitHub Pages for free, then point your GoDaddy DNS at it:
- Push your `index.html` to a GitHub repository and enable GitHub Pages in the repo Settings.
- In your GoDaddy account, navigate to **Manage Domains**, scroll to your domain, click through, scroll down and select **Manage DNS**. Add a CNAME record where the Host is `www` and Points To is `[your-username].github.io`.

---

## What You Need From Me

To get the page actually uploaded, I need to either:
- Pull it from the previous session where I built it (let me search for it if you do not have the file), **or**
- Rebuild it now so you have a clean `index.html` file ready to upload.

But the terms “churches” and “religious organizations” are used somewhat differently by the IRS. Understanding these differences is important for religious groups seeking 501(c) (3) tax-exempt status because different tax rules and reporting requirements apply to each. For federal tax purposes, a church is any recognized place of worship—including synagogues, mosques, and temples—regardless of its adherents’ faith or religious belief. The IRS automatically recognizes churches as 501(c) (3) charitable organizations if they meet the IRS requirements. There is no need for churches to seek formal recognition from the IRS or submit annual information returns (though they have the option to do so). 

Instead of providing a single definition that applies to all cases, the IRS uses a combination of characteristics to identify churches—including having distinct forms of worship, creeds, literature, religious history, and ecclesiastical government.

But like churches and other charitable organizations, religious organizations must meet the following requirements to qualify for 501(c) (3) federal tax-exempt status: the organization must organize and operate exclusively for the pursuit of one or more charitable purposes recognized by the IRS; the organization’s net earnings must not serve to enrich private individuals or shareholders (beyond reasonable compensation for services rendered); lobbying cannot make up a substantial part of the organization’s activities; the organization cannot intervene in political campaigns; and · the organization’s purpose and actions cannot be illegal or violate fundamental public policy.

Here we go. Every single step, nothing skipped.

---

## Part 1 — Create a GitHub Account

1. Open a browser and go to **github.com**
2. Click **Sign up** in the top right corner
3. Enter your email address, create a password, choose a username
4. Verify you're human (the puzzle thing)
5. Click **Create account**
6. GitHub sends a verification code to your email — go to your email, copy the code, paste it back into GitHub
7. It asks some questions about your use — you can skip all of them
8. You are now on your GitHub dashboard

---

## Part 2 — Create a Repository (this is just a folder that holds your site)

1. Click the **+** icon in the top right corner
2. Click **New repository**
3. In the **Repository name** box, type exactly: `yourusername.github.io` — replace "yourusername" with the actual username you just created (has to match exactly)
4. Make sure **Public** is selected
5. Check the box that says **Add a README file**
6. Click **Create repository**

---

## Part 3 — Upload Your HTML File

1. You are now inside your repository
2. Click **Add file** (near the top)
3. Click **Upload files**
4. Drag your HTML file onto the page, or click **choose your files** and find it on your computer
5. The file **must be named** `index.html` — if it's named something else, rename it on your computer first before uploading
6. Scroll down and click **Commit changes**

---

## Part 4 — Turn On GitHub Pages

1. Click **Settings** (tab at the top of your repository)
2. In the left sidebar, click **Pages**
3. Under **Branch**, click the dropdown that says **None** and change it to **main**
4. Click **Save**
5. Wait about 2 minutes
6. Refresh the page — you will see a green bar that says **Your site is live at** `https://yourusername.github.io`
7. Click that link to confirm your site is up

---

## Part 5 — Point Your GoDaddy Domain At It

1. Log into **godaddy.com**
2. Click your account icon, then **My Products**
3. Find your domain and click **DNS** next to it
4. You will see a list of existing DNS records
5. Find the record with **Type: CNAME** and **Name: www** — click the pencil icon to edit it
6. Change the **Value** field to `yourusername.github.io`
7. Click **Save**
8. Now look for the **A record** with **Name: @** — if there is one, delete it (click the trash icon)
9. Click **Add New Record**

Managing a custom domain for your GitHub Pages site

You can set up or update certain DNS records and your repository settings to point the default domain for your GitHub Pages site to a custom domain.

Who can use this feature?

GitHub Pages is available in public repositories with GitHub Free and GitHub Free for organizations, and in public and private repositories with GitHub Pro, GitHub Team, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Server. For more information, see GitHub’s plans.

Platform navigation

People with admin permissions for a repository can configure a custom domain for a GitHub Pages site.

About custom domain configuration

Tip

We recommend verifying your custom domain prior to adding it to your repository, in order to improve security and avoid takeover attacks. For more information, see Verifying your custom domain for GitHub Pages.



Make sure you add your custom domain to your GitHub Pages site before configuring your custom domain with your DNS provider. Configuring your custom domain with your DNS provider without adding your custom domain to GitHub could result in someone else being able to host a site on one of your subdomains.

The dig command, which can be used to verify correct configuration of DNS records, is not included in Windows. To verify that your DNS records are configured correctly, you can use the Resolve-DnsName PowerShell command or install BIND.

Note

DNS changes can take up to 24 hours to propagate.

Configuring an apex domain

To set up an apex domain, such as example.com, you must configure a custom domain in your repository settings and at least one ALIAS, ANAME, or A record with your DNS provider.

DomainSettingGuide

How to Connect a Custom Domain to GitHub Pages

Follow these steps to purchase a custom domain and connect it to your GitHub Pages site.

  1. Purchase a Custom Domain

    • Visit a domain provider to purchase a domain of your choice (e.g., example.com).
    • After purchasing, you’ll have access to the domain's settings, including DNS configuration, which will be needed in later steps.
  2. Enable GitHub Pages

    • Go to the Settings tab of your GitHub repository.
    • Select Pages from the left menu.
    • Under Source, choose the branch you want to deploy (typically main or gh-pages) and the directory (/root or /docs).
    • Once selected, GitHub will generate a default URL (username.github.io/repository-name) for your site.
  3. Set Up Your Custom Domain



    • In the GitHub Pages settings, under Custom domain, enter your custom domain (e.g., www.example.com) and save.
  4. Configure DNS Settings

    • Log in to your domain provider (e.g., GoDaddy, Cloudflare) and update the DNS settings as follows:
      • Add A records pointing to the following GitHub IP addresses:
        • 185.199.108.153
        • 185.199.109.153
        • 185.199.110.153
        • 185.199.111.153
      • If you’re using a subdomain (e.g., www.example.com), add a CNAME record pointing to username.github.io.
  5. Enable HTTPS (Optional)

    • After DNS propagation, return to your GitHub Pages settings and enable Enforce HTTPS for secure access.

Note: DNS settings may take up to 24 hours to propagate.

Once these steps are complete, your GitHub Pages site should be accessible through your custom domain!

Masking is a popular option when you want to keep your domain in the browser address bar and you aren't concerned about SEO or search engine results. Search engines don't index any information about the destination URL or retain any previous details from your domain after setting up masking. Instead, you'll need to provide specific meta-tags for search engines to read, including a title, description and keywords that'll be associated with your domain. Since there isn't a specific website to index, the overall search engine ranking performance for your domain won't be as good as a 301 or 302 redirect. 

Some destination URLs don't support masking, which could lead to visitors seeing a blank white screen instead of the destination website. This is controlled by the destination URL and isn't something GoDaddy is able to solve, unfortunately. If you encounter this issue, the only way to fix it is to change your forwarding type to a 301 or 302 redirect.

If you are forwarding and masking in Godaddy, here are a few things you should know. Search engines only see the real url of the websites and pages. Although visitors may see olddomain.com because of masking, this does not apply to search engines. Search engines see and index results for newdomain.com since that’s the actual domain for the website. Masking only works if visitors specifically go to olddomain.com. If they reach newdomain.com in some other way, such as a Google search, then that’s what they will see in their browser. There’s no retroactive way to make the website appear under olddomain.com. Forwarded domains offer no search engine value. Some folks mistakenly think that if they buy 10 domains and forward them all to the same website, then all 10 domains could appear in search results and dominate a keyword search result. The reality is, only the domain that a website actually lives on will be indexed and offer SEO value.



If you purchased a domain through Godaddy, you can point that domain to a specific IP address (for website hosting) or have it forwarded to another url. For forwarding, there are a few options to consider and your settings depend on your particular needs. Below is an overview of domain forwarding and masking options in Godaddy. There are two types of domain forwarding. Permanent redirects are typically used when you have changed your website domain. For instance, if your website used to be olddomain.com but is changing to newdomain.com, then you will want to permanently forward the old domain to the new one. This also tells search engines that you want them to index the new domain and replace references to the old one. Conversely, temporary redirects tell search engines that you wish to keep indexing for the current domain, even though it’s being forwarded to another.



Your selections impact both SEO and visitor experience, so be sure to keep this in mind when selecting among the domain forwarding and masking options in Go

content.text:
1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill                           |
    60	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
    61	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `/mnt/skills/public/pdf-reading/SKILL.md` |
    62	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `/mnt/skills/public/docx/SKILL.md`        |
    63	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `/mnt/skills/public/docx/SKILL.md`        |
    64	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    65	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    66	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    67	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `/mnt/skills/public/xlsx/SKILL.md`        |
    68	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md`        |
    69	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md`        |
    70	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)                                 |
    71	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)                                 |
    72	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)                                 |
    73	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)                                 |
    74	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)                                 |
    75	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)                                 |
    76	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)                                 |
    77	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)                                 |
    78	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)                                 |
    79	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —                                         |
    80	
    81	---
    82	
    83	## PDF
    84	
    85	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    86	
    87	Quick first move — get the page count and check if text is extractable:
    88	
    89	```bash
    90	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    91	pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
    92	```
    93	
    94	Then peek at the text content:
    95	
    96	```python
    97	from pypdf import PdfReader
    98	r = PdfReader("/mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf")
    99	print(f"{len(r.pages)} pages")
   100	print(r.pages[0].extract_text()[:2000])
   101	```
   102	
   103	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   104	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   105	— go read `/mnt/skills/public/pdf-reading/SKILL.md`. It covers
   106	content inventory, text extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded
   107	content extraction, and document-type-aware reading strategies.
   108	
   109	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   110	go read `/mnt/skills/public/pdf/SKILL.md`.
   111	
   112	---
   113	
   114	## DOCX / DOC
   115	
   116	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   117	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   118	
   119	```bash
   120	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   121	```
   122	
   123	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   124	skill.
   125	
   126	---
   127	
   128	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   129	
   130	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   131	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   132	
   133	```bash
   134	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   135	```
   136	
   137	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   138	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   139	
   140	```python
   141	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   142	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   143	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   144	ws = wb.active
   145	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   146	    print(row)
   147	```
   148	
   149	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   150	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   151	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   152	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   153	count, iterate or use pandas.
   154	
   155	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   156	
   157	```python
   158	import pandas as pd
   159	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   160	```
   161	
   162	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   163	
   164	```python
   165	import pandas as pd
   166	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   167	```
   168	
   169	---
   170	
   171	## PPTX
   172	
   173	```bash
   174	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   175	```
   176	
   177	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see
   178	`/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md` for the sandbox-safe
   179	`scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper (bare `soffice` hangs here because
   180	the seccomp filter blocks the `AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for
   181	instance management).
   182	
   183	For anything beyond reading, go to `/mnt/skills/public/pptx/SKILL.md`.
   184	
   185	---
   186	
   187	## CSV / TSV
   188	
   189	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   190	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   191	
   192	```python
   193	import pandas as pd
   194	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   195	print(df)
   196	print()
   197	print(df.dtypes)
   198	```
   199	
   200	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   201	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   202	warned about above):
   203	
   204	```bash
   205	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   206	```
   207	
   208	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   209	
   210	```python
   211	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   212	print(df.describe())
   213	```
   214	
   215	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   216	
   217	---
   218	
   219	## JSON / JSONL
   220	
   221	Structure first, content second:
   222	
   223	```bash
   224	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   225	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   226	```
   227	
   228	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   229	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   230	
   231	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   232	
   233	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   234	by line:
   235	
   236	```bash
   237	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   238	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   239	```
   240	
   241	---
   242	
   243	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   244	
   245	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   246	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   247	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   248	
   249	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   250	programmatically:
   251	
   252	```python
   253	from PIL import Image
   254	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   255	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   256	```
   257	
   258	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   259	
   260	```python
   261	import pytesseract
   262	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   263	```
   264	
   265	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   266	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   267	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   268	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   269	
   270	---
   271	
   272	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   273	
   274	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   275	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   276	
   277	```bash
   278	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   279	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   280	```
   281	
   282	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   283	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   284	
   285	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   286	
   287	```bash
   288	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   289	```
   290	
   291	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   292	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   293	
   294	```bash
   295	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   296	```
   297	
   298	---
   299	
   300	## EPUB / ODT
   301	
   302	```bash
   303	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/book.epub | head -200
   304	```
   305	
   306	For long ebooks, pipe through `head` — you rarely need the whole thing
   307	to answer a question.
   308	
   309	---
   310	
   311	## RTF / IPYNB
   312	
   313	```bash
   314	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notes.rtf | head -200
   315	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notebook.ipynb | head -200
   316	```
   317	
   318	---
   319	
   320	## Plain text / code / logs
   321	
   322	Check the size first:
   323	
   324	```bash
   325	wc -c /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   326	```
   327	
   328	- **Under ~20KB**: `cat` is fine.
   329	- **Over ~20KB**: `head -100` and `tail -100` to orient. If the user
   330	  asked about something specific, `grep` for it. Load the whole thing
   331	  only if you genuinely need all of it.
   332	
   333	For log files, the user almost always cares about the end:
   334	
   335	```bash
   336	tail -200 /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   337	```
   338	
   339	---
   340	
   341	## Unknown extension
   342	
   343	```bash
   344	file /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin
   345	xxd /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin | head -5
   346	```
   347	
   348	`file` identifies most things. `xxd` head shows magic bytes. If `file`
   349	says "data" and the hex doesn't match anything you recognize, ask the
   350	user what it is instead of guessing.

THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE
 Austin, Texas · Established under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
 FOUNDING BOARD RESOLUTION
 Action of the Initial Board of Directors Without a Formal Meeting
Pursuant to the authority granted by the Bylaws of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute (hereinafter "the
Institute"), the undersigned, constituting the entire initial Board of Directors of the Institute, hereby adopts the
following resolutions by written consent in lieu of a formal organizational meeting, effective as of the date set
forth below.
DATE OF ACTION
On this 
 day of 
, 
, the initial Board of Directors of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute,
duly convened and acting by written consent, hereby adopts the following resolutions.
RECITALS
WHEREAS, the founders of the Institute have determined to establish a Faith-Based Organization under the
laws of the State of Texas and pursuant to the automatic tax exemption afforded by 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A),
for the purpose of restoring displaced workers to the dignity of productive, skilled, and purposeful labor in
obedience to the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10;
WHEREAS, the founders have prepared and adopted a Theological Framework setting forth the scriptural,
historical, and doctrinal foundations of the Institute, a Statement of Faith setting forth the sincere religious
convictions of this organization, and Bylaws governing the internal operations of the Institute;
WHEREAS, the Bylaws provide for an initial Board of Directors consisting of the Founder, and authorize the
Board to act by written consent without a formal meeting;
WHEREAS, the Board has reviewed the Theological Framework, the Statement of Faith, and the Bylaws,
and desires to formally adopt these documents, appoint officers, designate the Minister's housing allowance,
and authorize the Institute to obtain an Employer Identification Number and open financial accounts; and
WHEREAS, all actions taken herein are consistent with and in furtherance of the theological mission of the
Institute as set forth in the governing documents;

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Board of Directors hereby adopts the following resolutions,
effective as of the date set forth above:
RESOLUTIONS
RESOLUTION 1 — ADOPTION OF THEOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK
RESOLVED, that the Theological Framework of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, as prepared and
presented to the Board, is hereby adopted in its entirety as a foundational governing document of the
Institute, and the officers of the Institute are authorized and directed to execute the same on behalf of
the Institute.
RESOLUTION 2 — ADOPTION OF STATEMENT OF FAITH
RESOLVED, that the Statement of Faith of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, as prepared and
presented to the Board, is hereby adopted in its entirety as the governing doctrinal confession of the
Institute, and the officers are authorized and directed to execute the same on behalf of the Institute.
RESOLUTION 3 — ADOPTION OF BYLAWS
RESOLVED, that the Bylaws of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, as prepared and presented to the
Board, are hereby adopted in their entirety as the governing Bylaws of the Institute, and the officers are
authorized and directed to execute the same on behalf of the Institute.
RESOLUTION 4 — APPOINTMENT OF MINISTER AND CHIEF EXECUTIVE
RESOLVED, that Rickey Jay Bennett II is hereby appointed as Minister and Chief Executive of The
Thessalonian Mandate Institute, to serve in that capacity until a successor is duly appointed, with all
authority granted to the Minister under the Bylaws and the governing documents of the Institute,
including eligibility for the minister's housing allowance under 26 U.S.C. § 107.
RESOLUTION 5 — DESIGNATION OF MINISTER'S HOUSING ALLOWANCE
RESOLVED, that pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 107 and the authority granted by the Bylaws, the Board
hereby designates one hundred percent (100%) of the compensation paid to Rickey Jay Bennett II as
Minister of the Institute to be a housing allowance, to the extent that such amount does not exceed: (a)
the actual cost of providing a home; (b) the fair rental value of the home, including furnishings and
appurtenances such as a garage, plus the cost of utilities; or (c) an amount which represents
reasonable pay for the Minister's services. This designation is effective as of the date of this Resolution
and shall remain in effect until amended or revoked by the Board.

RESOLUTION 6 — APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY AND TREASURER
RESOLVED, that Rickey Jay Bennett II is hereby appointed to serve additionally as Secretary and
Treasurer of the Institute until such time as additional officers are appointed by the Board, it being
understood that a sole Director may hold multiple offices under the Bylaws of this organization.
RESOLUTION 7 — AUTHORIZATION TO OBTAIN EMPLOYER IDENTIFICATION NUMBER
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized and directed to apply for and obtain an Employer
Identification Number (EIN) from the Internal Revenue Service on behalf of The Thessalonian Mandate
Institute, and to execute all forms and certifications necessary to complete such application, including
IRS Form SS-4 or any online equivalent thereof.
RESOLUTION 8 — AUTHORIZATION TO OPEN FINANCIAL ACCOUNTS
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized to open one or more bank accounts, credit accounts,
and other financial accounts in the name of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, to designate
signatories on such accounts, and to execute all documents required by any financial institution in
connection therewith.
RESOLUTION 9 — AUTHORIZATION TO APPLY FOR GRANTS AND GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized to identify, apply for, and accept grants, government
contracts, and other funding opportunities on behalf of the Institute in furtherance of its theological
mission, and to execute all applications, agreements, and certifications required in connection therewith.
RESOLUTION 10 — AUTHORIZATION TO HOLD INSURANCE POLICIES AS TREASURY INSTRUMENT
RESOLVED, that the Institute is hereby authorized, consistent with Section 6.3 of the Bylaws, to acquire
and hold one or more whole life insurance policies as an asset of the organization, to use the cash value
thereof as an operating reserve and treasury instrument, and to borrow against such policies in
furtherance of the mission of the Institute, subject to such terms and conditions as the Minister shall
determine to be in the best interest of the Institute.
RESOLUTION 11 — PRINCIPAL OFFICE
RESOLVED, that the principal office of the Institute shall be located in Austin, Travis County, Texas, at
such address as the Minister shall designate, and the Minister is authorized to establish such address
and to maintain or change the same as the needs of the Institute may require.
RESOLUTION 12 — REGISTERED AGENT
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized to designate a registered agent for the Institute in the
State of Texas and to take all steps necessary to maintain such designation in compliance with
applicable Texas law.

===== TMI_Bylaws-1.pdf =====
THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE
 Austin, Texas · Established under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
 BYLAWS
 A Faith-Based Organization — 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
PREAMBLE
These Bylaws govern the internal operations of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, a Faith-Based
Organization operating under the automatic tax exemption provided by 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A). This
organization is not a 501(c)(3) organization and has not applied for IRS determination. Its exempt status
derives directly and automatically from the Internal Revenue Code applicable to faith-based organizations.
All operations are subordinate to the theological convictions set forth in the Statement of Faith and the
Theological Framework of this organization.
ARTICLE I
— NAME, NATURE, AND PRINCIPAL OFFICE
Section 1.1. Name
The name of this organization is The Thessalonian Mandate Institute (hereinafter "the Institute" or "the
Organization").
Section 1.2. Nature
The Institute is a Faith-Based Organization operating pursuant to the sincere religious convictions of its
founders and leadership, as set forth in its Statement of Faith. The Institute holds that the obligation to work
is a divine mandate rooted in scripture, and that equipping displaced workers with the skills necessary to
fulfill that mandate is an act of religious ministry. All programs, activities, and operations flow from and are
governed by this theological conviction.
Section 1.3. Principal Office
The principal office of the Institute shall be located in Austin, Travis County, Texas. The Board of Directors
may change the principal office or establish additional offices as ministry needs require.
Section 1.4. Registered Agent

The Institute shall maintain a registered agent in the State of Texas as required by applicable law. The
identity of the registered agent may be changed by resolution of the Board of Directors.
ARTICLE II
— MISSION AND PURPOSE
Section 2.1. Primary Mission
The primary mission of the Institute is to restore displaced workers to the dignity of productive, skilled, and
purposeful labor by equipping them with the technical knowledge and professional capabilities necessary to
participate fully in the modern economy — in obedience to the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 and in
fulfillment of the theological standard of skilled excellence set forth in Proverbs 22:29.
Section 2.2. Theological Purpose
The Institute understands the mass displacement of workers by automation and artificial intelligence as a
spiritual crisis — a crisis of vocation — that demands a theological response. All activities of the Institute are
conducted as acts of religious ministry, grounded in the sincere theological convictions of its founders.
Section 2.3. Program Purpose
In furtherance of its mission, the Institute may engage in the following activities:
1. Providing instruction in technology fields including information technology, cybersecurity, cloud
computing, data analysis, and AI-assisted workflow management;
2. Developing and delivering curriculum aligned with industry-recognized certification pathways;
3. Establishing cohort-based learning communities that provide mutual support and accountability to
participants;
4. Providing job placement assistance, mentorship, and post-program support to graduates;
5. Conducting research, publishing, and public education on the theological dimensions of work,
vocation, and technological displacement;
6. Receiving donations, grants, and other contributions in support of the foregoing activities;
7. Acquiring, holding, and managing property and assets in furtherance of the mission; and
8. Engaging in any other activity consistent with the theological mission of the Institute.
Section 2.4. Non-Discrimination in Program Participation
The Institute shall admit participants to its programs without regard to race, color, national origin, sex, age, or
disability. The Institute may, consistent with its religious convictions, establish program requirements related
to conduct, commitment, and participation that apply uniformly to all participants.
ARTICLE III
— THEOLOGICAL GOVERNANCE
Section 3.1. Supremacy of Theological Foundation

The Statement of Faith and the Theological Framework of the Institute are the supreme governing
documents with respect to matters of doctrine, mission, and religious conviction. No action of the Board, the
Minister, or any officer shall contradict, undermine, or depart from the theological foundations of the Institute.
Section 3.2. Minister Designation
The founder and Chief Executive of the Institute shall hold the title of Minister and shall be recognized as the
primary religious leader of this organization for all purposes, including eligibility for the minister's housing
allowance under 26 U.S.C. § 107. The Board of Directors may designate additional persons as Ministers of
the Institute as ministry needs require.
Section 3.3. Religious Liberty Protection
The Institute claims the full protection of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and of all
applicable federal and state religious liberty statutes in the conduct of its operations. The Institute shall not
be required to act contrary to its sincerely held religious convictions in any aspect of its operations.
Section 3.4. Faith-Based Hiring
Consistent with its status as a faith-based organization and the protections afforded by applicable law, the
Institute may require that all employees, contractors, and volunteers affirm the Statement of Faith and
commit to conduct their service in a manner consistent with the theological convictions of the Institute.
ARTICLE IV
— BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Section 4.1. Authority
The Board of Directors (hereinafter "the Board") shall be the governing body of the Institute, responsible for
oversight of the organization's operations, finances, and strategic direction, subject to the theological
supremacy established in Article III.
Section 4.2. Composition
The Board shall consist of not fewer than one (1) and not more than seven (7) Directors. The initial Board
shall consist of the Founder, who shall serve as sole Director until additional Directors are appointed. The
Board may increase or decrease the number of Directors by resolution, within these limits.
Section 4.3. Qualifications
All Directors must: (a) be at least eighteen (18) years of age; (b) affirm the Statement of Faith; (c) commit to

 Austin, Texas · Established under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
 FOUNDING STORY AND MINISTER
 BIOGRAPHY
 For Public Distribution, Grant Applications, and Organizational Records
THE FOUNDING STORY
For eleven years, Rickey Jay Bennett II preached the Word of God on the streets of
America.
Not from a pulpit. Not with a salary or a congregation or a denominational charter behind her. She preached
from sidewalks and shelters and bus stations, in cities from one coast to the other, as a traveling minister
without credentials or institutional backing — only a Bible and a conviction that would not leave her alone.
The conviction was this: that work is sacred. That the capacity for productive, skilled, dignified labor is not a
feature of economic life but a feature of human nature — given by a Creator God who worked in the
beginning, before sin entered the world, before the sweat and the thorns. That the man or woman who is
willing to work and cannot is not facing an economic problem. They are facing a spiritual crisis. A violation of
something God intended.
She knew this not because she had studied it in seminary. She knew it because she was living it.
For twenty-three years, Rickey Bennett navigated homelessness, instability, and the particular cruelty of a
labor market that can strip a willing worker of every foothold before they can find the next one. She lost jobs
as quickly as she found them. She preached the dignity of labor from the exact position of someone the
economy had left behind — not despite the contradiction, but because of it. Because she understood from
the inside what it means to be willing, to be able, to be trying, and still to be without.
And then one day she put the book down.
Not with anger. Not with a declaration. She simply stopped picking it up. After twenty-three years of living the
problem and eleven years of preaching at it, the gap between what the mandate promised and what the
world delivered had become too wide to keep standing in. The reassurance that God would provide had

grown hollow — not because it was false, but because provision requires more than proclamation. It requires
action. It requires someone to build the thing that should have already existed.
The Thessalonian Mandate Institute is that thing.
It was not born in a boardroom or a seminary or a nonprofit incubator. It was born in the understanding that
the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 is not a comfort. It is a command — and a command carries with
it a corresponding obligation. If those who are willing to work must work, then the community of faith must
ensure they have the capacity to do so. When technology displaces a worker from their vocation, the Church
does not get to offer thoughts and prayers. The Church is obligated to equip.
Rickey Bennett built this organization because she spent two decades on the other side of that obligation,
waiting for someone to fulfill it. She is building it so that the next generation of displaced workers does not
have to wait as long.
The mandate stands. Now we build.
MINISTER BIOGRAPHY — FORMAL
For grant applications, official correspondence, and organizational materials
Rickey Jay Bennett II is the Founder and Minister of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, a Faith-Based
Organization established in Austin, Texas, under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A), dedicated to the workforce
retraining of individuals displaced by automation and artificial intelligence.
Minister Bennett brings to this work a singular combination of lived experience, theological conviction, and
organizational vision. An independent minister and street preacher for over eleven years, she proclaimed the
scriptural mandate of dignified labor across the United States while navigating the very conditions of
economic displacement that the Institute exists to address. Her ministry was conducted without institutional
affiliation or denominational support — grounded entirely in scripture and sustained by sincere religious
conviction.
Her theological framework centers on the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10, read within the broader
biblical tradition of vocation that extends from the creation mandate of Genesis 2:15 through the wisdom
tradition of Proverbs and the apostolic teaching of Paul. She understands technological displacement not as
an economic phenomenon but as a spiritual crisis — a forcible removal of human beings from the vocation
God assigned them at creation — and has constructed a comprehensive doctrinal response to that crisis in
the founding documents of the Institute.
Minister Bennett is an independent researcher and writer whose work spans artificial intelligence, philosophy
of mind, and the theology of human labor. She publishes under her legal name and has developed a body of
theoretical work addressing the intersection of technology and human dignity. Her approach to the Institute's
mission reflects both the rigor of her intellectual formation and the urgency of her personal experience.

She serves as Minister, Chief Executive, Secretary, and Treasurer of the Institute, and as the sole initial
member of its Board of Directors.
MINISTER BIOGRAPHY — SHORT
For website, press materials, and introductions
Rickey Jay Bennett II is the Founder and Minister of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute. She preached the
dignity of labor on the streets of America for eleven years — without a pulpit, without credentials, without
institutional backing — while navigating the same economic displacement her organization now exists to
address. She founded the Institute on the conviction that the work mandate of scripture is not a comfort but a
command, and that the community of faith is obligated to equip those who are willing to work but cannot. She
is based in Austin, Texas.
NOTE ON MINISTER'S IDENTITY
Minister Bennett is a transgender woman. This is stated plainly because plain statement is the only treatment
consistent with the dignity her organization preaches.
The Institute serves anyone willing to work. Its minister is someone who has spent a lifetime navigating a
world that did not always make space for her — which is precisely why she understands what it means to be
displaced from your vocation by forces beyond your control. Her identity is not incidental to the mission. It is
evidence that the mandate applies without exception, that dignity in labor belongs to everyone the economy
has left behind, and that the God who commands work does not first require conformity.
The work is real. The theology is sound. The minister is who she is.

 Austin, Texas · 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)

 FOUNDING BOARD RESOLUTION
 Action of the Initial Board of Directors Without a Formal Meeting
Pursuant to the authority granted by the Bylaws of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute (hereinafter "the
Institute"), the undersigned, constituting the entire initial Board of Directors of the Institute, hereby adopts the
following resolutions by written consent in lieu of a formal organizational meeting, effective as of the date set
forth below.
DATE OF ACTION
On this 
 day of 
, 
, the initial Board of Directors of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute,
duly convened and acting by written consent, hereby adopts the following resolutions.
RECITALS
WHEREAS, the founders of the Institute have determined to establish a Faith-Based Organization under the
laws of the State of Texas and pursuant to the automatic tax exemption afforded by 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A),
for the purpose of restoring displaced workers to the dignity of productive, skilled, and purposeful labor in
obedience to the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10;
WHEREAS, the founders have prepared and adopted a Theological Framework setting forth the scriptural,
historical, and doctrinal foundations of the Institute, a Statement of Faith setting forth the sincere religious
convictions of this organization, and Bylaws governing the internal operations of the Institute;
WHEREAS, the Bylaws provide for an initial Board of Directors consisting of the Founder, and authorize the
Board to act by written consent without a formal meeting;
WHEREAS, the Board has reviewed the Theological Framework, the Statement of Faith, and the Bylaws,
and desires to formally adopt these documents, appoint officers, designate the Minister's housing allowance,
and authorize the Institute to obtain an Employer Identification Number and open financial accounts; and
WHEREAS, all actions taken herein are consistent with and in furtherance of the theological mission of the
Institute as set forth in the governing documents;

effective as of the date set forth above:
RESOLUTIONS
RESOLUTION 1 — ADOPTION OF THEOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK
RESOLVED, that the Theological Framework of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, as prepared and
presented to the Board, is hereby adopted in its entirety as a foundational governing document of the
Institute, and the officers of the Institute are authorized and directed to execute the same on behalf of
the Institute.
RESOLUTION 2 — ADOPTION OF STATEMENT OF FAITH
RESOLVED, that the Statement of Faith of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, as prepared and
presented to the Board, is hereby adopted in its entirety as the governing doctrinal confession of the
Institute, and the officers are authorized and directed to execute the same on behalf of the Institute.
RESOLUTION 3 — ADOPTION OF BYLAWS
RESOLVED, that the Bylaws of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, as prepared and presented to the
Board, are hereby adopted in their entirety as the governing Bylaws of the Institute, and the officers are
authorized and directed to execute the same on behalf of the Institute.
RESOLUTION 4 — APPOINTMENT OF MINISTER AND CHIEF EXECUTIVE
RESOLVED, that Rickey Jay Bennett II is hereby appointed as Minister and Chief Executive of The
Thessalonian Mandate Institute, to serve in that capacity until a successor is duly appointed, with all
authority granted to the Minister under the Bylaws and the governing documents of the Institute,
including eligibility for the minister's housing allowance under 26 U.S.C. § 107.
RESOLUTION 5 — DESIGNATION OF MINISTER'S HOUSING ALLOWANCE
RESOLVED, that pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 107 and the authority granted by the Bylaws, the Board
hereby designates one hundred percent (100%) of the compensation paid to Rickey Jay Bennett II as
Minister of the Institute to be a housing allowance, to the extent that such amount does not exceed: (a)
the actual cost of providing a home; (b) the fair rental value of the home, including furnishings and
appurtenances such as a garage, plus the cost of utilities; or (c) an amount which represents
reasonable pay for the Minister's services. This designation is effective as of the date of this Resolution
and shall remain in effect until amended or revoked by the Board.

RESOLUTION 6 — APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY AND TREASURER
RESOLVED, that Rickey Jay Bennett II is hereby appointed to serve additionally as Secretary and
Treasurer of the Institute until such time as additional officers are appointed by the Board, it being
understood that a sole Director may hold multiple offices under the Bylaws of this organization.
RESOLUTION 7 — AUTHORIZATION TO OBTAIN EMPLOYER IDENTIFICATION NUMBER
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized and directed to apply for and obtain an Employer
Identification Number (EIN) from the Internal Revenue Service on behalf of The Thessalonian Mandate
Institute, and to execute all forms and certifications necessary to complete such application, including
IRS Form SS-4 or any online equivalent thereof.
RESOLUTION 8 — AUTHORIZATION TO OPEN FINANCIAL ACCOUNTS
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized to open one or more bank accounts, credit accounts,
and other financial accounts in the name of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, to designate
signatories on such accounts, and to execute all documents required by any financial institution in
connection therewith.
RESOLUTION 9 — AUTHORIZATION TO APPLY FOR GRANTS AND GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized to identify, apply for, and accept grants, government
contracts, and other funding opportunities on behalf of the Institute in furtherance of its theological
mission, and to execute all applications, agreements, and certifications required in connection therewith.
RESOLUTION 10 — AUTHORIZATION TO HOLD INSURANCE POLICIES AS TREASURY INSTRUMENT
RESOLVED, that the Institute is hereby authorized, consistent with Section 6.3 of the Bylaws, to acquire
and hold one or more whole life insurance policies as an asset of the organization, to use the cash value
thereof as an operating reserve and treasury instrument, and to borrow against such policies in
furtherance of the mission of the Institute, subject to such terms and conditions as the Minister shall
determine to be in the best interest of the Institute.
RESOLUTION 11 — PRINCIPAL OFFICE
RESOLVED, that the principal office of the Institute shall be located in Austin, Travis County, Texas, at
such address as the Minister shall designate, and the Minister is authorized to establish such address
and to maintain or change the same as the needs of the Institute may require.
RESOLUTION 12 — REGISTERED AGENT
RESOLVED, that the Minister is hereby authorized to designate a registered agent for the Institute in the
State of Texas and to take all steps necessary to maintain such designation in compliance with
applicable Texas law.

===== TMI_Bylaws-1.pdf =====
THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE
 Austin, Texas · Established under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
 BYLAWS
 A Faith-Based Organization — 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
PREAMBLE
These Bylaws govern the internal operations of The Thessalonian Mandate Institute, a Faith-Based
Organization operating under the automatic tax exemption provided by 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A). This
organization is not a 501(c)(3) organization and has not applied for IRS determination. Its exempt status
derives directly and automatically from the Internal Revenue Code applicable to faith-based organizations.
All operations are subordinate to the theological convictions set forth in the Statement of Faith and the
Theological Framework of this organization.
ARTICLE I
— NAME, NATURE, AND PRINCIPAL OFFICE
Section 1.1. Name
The name of this organization is The Thessalonian Mandate Institute (hereinafter "the Institute" or "the
Organization").
Section 1.2. Nature
The Institute is a Faith-Based Organization operating pursuant to the sincere religious convictions of its
founders and leadership, as set forth in its Statement of Faith. The Institute holds that the obligation to work
is a divine mandate rooted in scripture, and that equipping displaced workers with the skills necessary to
fulfill that mandate is an act of religious ministry. All programs, activities, and operations flow from and are
governed by this theological conviction.
Section 1.3. Principal Office
The principal office of the Institute shall be located in Austin, Travis County, Texas. The Board of Directors
may change the principal office or establish additional offices as ministry needs require.
Section 1.4. Registered Agent

The Institute shall maintain a registered agent in the State of Texas as required by applicable law. The
identity of the registered agent may be changed by resolution of the Board of Directors.
ARTICLE II
— MISSION AND PURPOSE
Section 2.1. Primary Mission
The primary mission of the Institute is to restore displaced workers to the dignity of productive, skilled, and
purposeful labor by equipping them with the technical knowledge and professional capabilities necessary to
participate fully in the modern economy — in obedience to the work mandate of 2 Thessalonians 3:10 and in
fulfillment of the theological standard of skilled excellence set forth in Proverbs 22:29.
Section 2.2. Theological Purpose
The Institute understands the mass displacement of workers by automation and artificial intelligence as a
spiritual crisis — a crisis of vocation — that demands a theological response. All activities of the Institute are
conducted as acts of religious ministry, grounded in the sincere theological convictions of its founders.
Section 2.3. Program Purpose
In furtherance of its mission, the Institute may engage in the following activities:
1. Providing instruction in technology fields including information technology, cybersecurity, cloud
computing, data analysis, and AI-assisted workflow management;
2. Developing and delivering curriculum aligned with industry-recognized certification pathways;
3. Establishing cohort-based learning communities that provide mutual support and accountability to
participants;
4. Providing job placement assistance, mentorship, and post-program support to graduates;
5. Conducting research, publishing, and public education on the theological dimensions of work,
vocation, and technological displacement;
6. Receiving donations, grants, and other contributions in support of the foregoing activities;
7. Acquiring, holding, and managing property and assets in furtherance of the mission; and
8. Engaging in any other activity consistent with the theological mission of the Institute.
Section 2.4. Non-Discrimination in Program Participation
The Institute shall admit participants to its programs without regard to race, color, national origin, sex, age, or
disability. The Institute may, consistent with its religious convictions, establish program requirements related
to conduct, commitment, and participation that apply uniformly to all participants.
ARTICLE III
— THEOLOGICAL GOVERNANCE
Section 3.1. Supremacy of Theological Foundation

The Statement of Faith and the Theological Framework of the Institute are the supreme governing
documents with respect to matters of doctrine, mission, and religious conviction. No action of the Board, the
Minister, or any officer shall contradict, undermine, or depart from the theological foundations of the Institute.
Section 3.2. Minister Designation
The founder and Chief Executive of the Institute shall hold the title of Minister and shall be recognized as the
primary religious leader of this organization for all purposes, including eligibility for the minister's housing
allowance under 26 U.S.C. § 107. The Board of Directors may designate additional persons as Ministers of
the Institute as ministry needs require.
Section 3.3. Religious Liberty Protection
The Institute claims the full protection of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution and of all
applicable federal and state religious liberty statutes in the conduct of its operations. The Institute shall not
be required to act contrary to its sincerely held religious convictions in any aspect of its operations.
Section 3.4. Faith-Based Hiring
Consistent with its status as a faith-based organization and the protections afforded by applicable law, the
Institute may require that all employees, contractors, and volunteers affirm the Statement of Faith and
commit to conduct their service in a manner consistent with the theological convictions of the Institute.
ARTICLE IV
— BOARD OF DIRECTORS
Section 4.1. Authority
The Board of Directors (hereinafter "the Board") shall be the governing body of the Institute, responsible for
oversight of the organization's operations, finances, and strategic direction, subject to the theological
supremacy established in Article III.
Section 4.2. Composition
The Board shall consist of not fewer than one (1) and not more than seven (7) Directors. The initial Board
shall consist of the Founder, who shall serve as sole Director until additional Directors are appointed. The
Board may increase or decrease the number of Directors by resolution, within these limits.
Section 4.3. Qualifications
All Directors must: (a) be at least eighteen (18) years of age; (b) affirm the Statement of Faith; (c) commit to
act in the best interest of the Institute and its mission; and (d) have no undisclosed conflict of interest that
would impair their ability to serve.
Section 4.4. Terms
Directors shall serve terms of two (2) years and may be re-appointed without limitation. Terms shall be
staggered where the Board has three or more Directors, so that continuity of governance is maintained.
Section 4.5. Appointment and Removal

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE
 Austin, Texas · Established under 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
 PROGRAM CURRICULUM OUTLINE
 Workforce Retraining for the Technologically Displaced
PROGRAM PHILOSOPHY
The Thessalonian Mandate Institute does not deliver curriculum — it delivers people to curriculum that
already exists, wraps that journey in community and theological purpose, and provides the case
management, accountability, and job placement support that free platforms cannot. This model keeps costs
minimal, scales efficiently, and positions the Institute as a shepherd and advocate rather than a content
producer.
Every pathway listed in this document is built on confirmed free or nonprofit-accessible training infrastructure.
No participant pays for instruction. The Institute's role is to recruit, assess, place, support, and connect —
and to ensure that the sacred obligation to equip the willing is fulfilled in practice, not just in principle.
FREE TRAINING INFRASTRUCTURE
The following platforms form the curriculum backbone of all Institute programs. Each is free to participants,
carries industry-recognized credentials, and is actively seeking nonprofit delivery partners.
IBM SkillsBuild — skillsbuild.org
1,000+ free courses. Cybersecurity, AI, cloud, data analytics, IT support, project management, workplace
readiness. IBM-branded digital credentials. Active nonprofit partnership program — the Institute qualifies to
apply.
Google Career Certificates — grow.google/certificates

America and Year Up. Hosted on Coursera with financial aid available.

Microsoft Learn — learn.microsoft.com

fundamentals, security. Leads to Microsoft certification pathways. Microsoft for Nonprofits program provides
additional resources and discounts.
Khan Academy — khanacademy.org
Free foundational instruction in math, reading, writing, computer basics, personal finance, and
entrepreneurship. Critical for participants who need foundational skill building before entering technical
pathways. No prerequisites. No time limits.
Coursera for Social Impact — coursera.org/social-impact

GCFGlobal (GCF Learn Free) — gcfglobal.org

The fastest entry point into technology employment. Help desk and IT support roles are available at every
organization of every size. Starting salary range $35,000–$55,000 in the Austin market.
Weekly Structure:
 Week 1–2: Digital foundations and computer hardware basics (GCFGlobal)

 Week 3–6: Networking, operating systems, and troubleshooting (Google IT Support)
 Week 7–10: Cybersecurity basics and IT support best practices (Google / IBM)
 Week 11–12: Resume preparation, mock interviews, job application support
Credentials Earned:
 Google IT Support Certificate (Coursera)

Cybersecurity Fundamentals — 10–14 weeks
One of the highest-demand fields in technology with a severe talent shortage. Entry-level cybersecurity roles
start at $50,000–$70,000. No prior IT experience required for the Google certificate pathway.
Weekly Structure:
 Week 1–3: Foundations of cybersecurity (Google Cybersecurity Certificate — Module 1)
 Week 4–6: Network security and vulnerability identification (Module 2–3)
 Week 7–10: Incident response, SIEM tools, and Python basics (Module 4–6)
 Week 11–12: Portfolio building and job application support
Credentials Earned:
 Google Cybersecurity Certificate
 IBM Cybersecurity Fundamentals Badge
Cloud Computing Fundamentals — 8–10 weeks
Cloud skills are required across virtually every technology role. Azure fundamentals is the most accessible
entry point and opens doors across Microsoft's entire ecosystem.
Weekly Structure:
 Week 1–2: Cloud concepts and service models (Microsoft Learn — AZ-900 Path)
 Week 3–5: Azure architecture, storage, and networking basics
 Week 6–8: Azure security, compliance, and governance
 Week 9–10: Exam preparation and certification attempt
Credentials Earned:
 Microsoft Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900)
 IBM Cloud Essentials Badge

Data Analytics — 12–16 weeks
Data skills are the most broadly applicable technical competency in the modern economy. Entry-level data
analyst roles pay $45,000–$65,000 and exist across every industry sector.
Weekly Structure:
 Week 1–3: Spreadsheet fundamentals and data organization (Google / GCFGlobal)
 Week 4–7: SQL basics and database querying (Google Data Analytics Certificate)
 Week 8–11: Data visualization with Tableau and Google Sheets
 Week 12–14: Capstone project and portfolio development
 Week 15–16: Job application support and employer introductions
Credentials Earned:
 Google Data Analytics Professional Certificate
 IBM Data Analyst Badge
AI Tools and Workflow Automation — 4–6 weeks
The most immediately practical pathway for workers displaced by AI specifically. Teaches participants to
work with AI tools rather than be replaced by them. Applicable across every industry and role type.
Weekly Structure:
 Week 1–2: AI fundamentals and how large language models work (IBM SkillsBuild)
 Week 3–4: Prompt engineering for workplace tasks (Anthropic / IBM)
 Week 5–6: Workflow automation tools and AI-assisted productivity
Credentials Earned:
 IBM AI Fundamentals Badge
 Anthropic AI Fluency Certificate
Microsoft Office and Administrative Technology — 4–8 weeks
The foundational pathway for participants moving into administrative, clerical, and office support roles. Broad
applicability across every employment sector.
Weekly Structure:

 Week 1–2: Word processing and document creation (GCFGlobal / MS Learn)
 Week 3–4: Spreadsheets and data organization (GCFGlobal / MS Learn)
 Week 5–6: Presentations and professional communication tools
 Week 7–8: Email, calendar management, and Microsoft 365 ecosystem
Credentials Earned:
 Microsoft Office Specialist Certification (exam-based)
 GCFGlobal Completion Certificate
NON-TECHNOLOGY PATHWAYS — DETAIL
Not every displaced worker is positioned for a technology career. The mandate applies equally to the factory
worker, the retail manager, the truck driver, and the office clerk. These pathways equip participants for
stable, dignified employment across a broad range of industries and skill levels.
Digital Literacy Foundations — 2–4 weeks · GCFGlobal / Khan Academy
For participants with minimal technology experience. Covers computer basics, internet navigation, email, and
smartphone proficiency. The prerequisite for every other pathway. No participant is turned away for lack of
baseline skills.
Topics Covered:
 Basic computer operation and file management
 Internet safety and email communication
 Smartphone and tablet proficiency
 Introduction to productivity tools
Financial Literacy and Personal Finance — 4–6 weeks · Khan Academy
Foundational financial knowledge that multiplies the value of every other pathway. Budgeting, banking,
credit, taxes, and benefits navigation. Especially critical for participants emerging from long-term
displacement.
Topics Covered:
 Budgeting and expense tracking
 Banking, savings, and credit fundamentals
 Tax basics and benefit programs

 Financial goal setting and planning
Small Business and Self-Employment Basics — 6–8 weeks · Khan Academy / Coursera
For participants whose best path to stability is self-employment. Covers business structure, basic
accounting, marketing, and customer acquisition. Pairs with the Institute's network of mentors and micro-loan
referrals.
Topics Covered:
 Business structure and legal basics
 Basic bookkeeping and record-keeping
 Marketing and customer acquisition fundamentals
 Pricing, invoicing, and cash flow management
Customer Service and Retail Skills — 3–4 weeks · Coursera / IBM SkillsBuild
High-demand skills across retail, hospitality, healthcare, and service industries. IBM's customer service
training leads to a recognized badge. Pairs with Institute employer network for direct placement.
Topics Covered:
 Communication and de-escalation skills
 Point of sale and transaction processing
 Customer relationship management basics
 Professional workplace conduct
Administrative and Office Professional — 6–8 weeks · MS Learn / GCFGlobal / LinkedIn Learning
Prepares participants for receptionist, administrative assistant, data entry, and office coordinator roles. One
of the broadest employment pipelines available to adult learners regardless of prior experience.
Topics Covered:
 Microsoft Word, Excel, and Outlook proficiency
 Business writing and professional communication
 Calendar and scheduling management
 Basic bookkeeping and records management

Workplace Readiness and Professional Skills — 2–4 weeks · IBM SkillsBuild
The foundational cohort orientation for all participants regardless of pathway. Covers professional conduct,
workplace communication, time management, and navigating workplace culture. IBM issues a recognized
digital badge upon completion.
Topics Covered:
 Professional communication and workplace norms
 Time management and task prioritization
 Conflict resolution and teamwork
 Job search strategy and interview preparation
English Language and Communication Skills — Ongoing · Khan Academy / GCFGlobal
Available as a standalone pathway or concurrent support for any other program. Reading, writing, and
professional communication for participants whose first language is not English or who need foundational
literacy support.
Topics Covered:
 Reading comprehension and vocabulary
 Business writing and professional email
 Verbal communication and presentation basics
 Grammar and mechanics for workplace documents
COHORT DELIVERY MODEL
All pathways are delivered in cohorts of 8–15 participants. The cohort model is not a logistical preference —
it is a theological conviction. Human beings were not created to learn alone, and community accountability is
one of the most powerful drivers of completion in adult workforce training.
Week 0 — Intake and Assessment
All participants complete intake, aptitude assessment, and pathway selection. Digital literacy baseline is
assessed. Participants without device access are connected to loaner devices through library and
community partnerships.

Week 1 — Cohort Orientation
All participants complete the IBM Workplace Readiness pathway together regardless of their individual track.
This builds cohort identity, establishes shared expectations, and provides an IBM digital credential
immediately.
Weeks 2–12 — Primary Pathway Training
Participants work through their individual pathway using the free platform infrastructure. Weekly cohort
check-ins provide accountability and peer support. Institute staff provide navigation support and
troubleshooting.
Final 2 Weeks — Portfolio and Placement
Resume building, LinkedIn profile creation, mock interviews, and direct connections to the Institute's
employer network. Certification exam support where applicable. Graduation and credential presentation.
Post-Graduation — Alumni Network
Graduates enter the Institute's alumni network and are encouraged to mentor incoming cohorts. This fulfills
the theological obligation of the equipped to equip others, and builds the organizational community over time.
PARTNERSHIP AND DONATION PIPELINE
The Institute actively pursues formal partnerships with the following organizations for curriculum donation,
access, and co-delivery:
IBM SkillsBuild
Nonprofit organization partnership — apply at skillsbuild.org/organizations-supporting-adult-learners.
Provides cohort-guided learning experiences, IBM credentials, and job fair access.
Google Career Certificates Fund
Nonprofit partnership through Merit America and Year Up frameworks. Contact grow.google/certificates for
nonprofit access programs.
Microsoft for Nonprofits
Free Microsoft 365 and Azure credits for qualifying nonprofits. The Institute qualifies upon receiving EIN.
Apply at microsoft.com/nonprofits.
Coursera for Social Impact
Free Coursera access for qualifying workforce development nonprofits. Apply at coursera.org/social-impact.

Goodwill Industries of Central Texas
Local Goodwill chapter operates its own workforce training programs and may partner for facility use,
referrals, and co-delivery.
Austin Public Library
Free LinkedIn Learning access for all cardholders. Computer access and device lending programs available
for participants without devices.
Austin Community College Continuing Education
ACC offers free and low-cost workforce training and may partner for facility use and credential alignment.
Per Scholas
National nonprofit delivering free tech training — potential referral and co-delivery partner rather than
competitor, as our populations overlap.
Workforce Solutions Capital Area
Austin-area workforce development board administering WIOA funds. Primary target for government contract
funding of program delivery.
 THE THESSALONIAN MANDATE INSTITUTE
 Austin, Texas · 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A)
 "The one who is willing to work shall be equipped to work."
